newsitem.title: USA: U.S. in "uncharted" heating oil waters - EIA chief.
newsitem.headline: U.S. in "uncharted" heating oil waters - EIA chief.

text.p: Although heating oil stocks are building and prices have fallen about 10 cents a gallon or 7 percent from recent five-year highs, the U.S. Energy Information Administration remains leery about the potential for supply disruptions or a price shock this winter.
"We are entering uncharted waters," said EIA administrator Jay Hakes.
This was "not necessarily to say this is an untenable situation," he said at the Energy Department's winter fuels conference.
"It's a set of circumstances that we don't have historical experience to deal with. We certainly may have ways to deal with it," he said.

Inventories of distillate, including heating oil and diesel, were holding about 16 percent lower than last year and about 20 percent lower than the five-year average for this time of year, partly because of strong demand for both products, not just heating oil.
EIA said if recent robust production continued, total U.S. distillate stocks might end November above 120 million barrels, just above the all-time low of 119.8 million barrels.

"We take little comfort in knowing this historical minimum occurred in 1989 -- the year in which an early cold spell drove heating oil prices up 21 cents per gallon from November to December," EIA said in a paper presented at the conference.

With oil prices remaining higher than the $20.18 EIA had assumed for the fourth quarter, the agency no longer held to its forecast that consumers were likely to pay about 8 cents a gallon more for heating oil this winter versus last winter.
"It would be hard to reach that average now," Hakes said.
With current residential prices about 23 cents a gallon higher than last year at this time, he said: "This scenario may be a little understated."
